highlights.title: Highlights
highlights.description:
Conway's refinement conjecture [LM24, Conj. 1.1.1(2)] asks whether every equation $ab=cd$ between omnific integers can be refined as $a=ef$, $b=gh$, $c=eg$, $d=fh$ with omnific integers $e,f,g,h$. For an integral domain this refinement property is the pre-Schreier property: every element is primal. Conway normal form, with the signs of the exponents reversed, identifies the omnific integers with $\mathbb Z+\mathbb R((\mathbf{No}^{<0}))_\kappa$, so the conjecture concerns generalised power series. The guide proves it, and more generally that $Z+R((G^{<0}))_\kappa$ is a pre-Schreier domain under hypotheses on the exponent group $G$ that contain conditions (A1)--(A3) of [LM24, Thm. 9.0.1]. The proof rests on four ideas.

Germs. Let $K$ be a field of characteristic zero, $G$ a Cauchy-complete ordered abelian group, and $J$ the ideal of series in $K((G^{\le0}))$ whose support is bounded away from $0$. The germ of $b$ at $\gamma$ is the class modulo $J$ of the translated truncation $b^{|\gamma}=t^{-\gamma}b_{|\gamma}$ [Ber00, Def. 6.1]. Germs satisfy Berarducci's convolution formula [Ber00, Lem. 7.5], and unless the germ of $b$ is a constant, the Cantor--Bendixson rank of $0$ in the closure of the support strictly decreases when $b$ is replaced by $b^{|\xi}$ for all $\xi<0$ sufficiently close to $0$.

Transcendence. Let $S$ be a subalgebra of $K((G^{\le0}))/J$ that is an integral domain and such that every element of $S$ is the germ of a series all of whose germs lie in $S$. Then the germ of a series whose germs at negative exponents lie in $S$, but which is not itself in $S$, is transcendental over $S$. Adjoining germs of minimal rank by transfinite recursion presents $K((G^{\le0}))/J$ as a polynomial ring over $K$. Hence $J$ is prime, which for $G=\mathbb R$ is Berarducci's theorem [Ber00, Cor. 9.8], and the ring of germs is a unique factorisation domain, which for $G=\mathbb R$ is Berarducci's conjecture as stated in [LM17, Conj. 1.5]. The same recursion with subalgebras of series closed under truncation presents $K((\mathbb R^{\le0}))$ as a polynomial ring over its subring of series with finite support, so $K((\mathbb R^{\le0}))$ is a GCD domain.

Reduction along Archimedean classes. Regrouping exponents along a convex subgroup $C$ writes $Z+R((G^{<0}))_\kappa$ as a $D+M$ construction inside $R((C))_\kappa((G/C)^{\le0})$, and a transfer lemma in the manner of [LM24, Lem. 9.2.1] reduces primality to primality of the regrouped series and of the restriction of the series to $C$. If the support meets finitely many Archimedean classes, $C$ is the ball below the leading class, the regrouped series has real exponents, and the GCD theorem applies. If it meets infinitely many, $C$ is the intersection of the balls of a limit family of classes; primality in the ring of germs over $G/C$, together with restriction of supports to Archimedean balls of $G/C$, gives primality by transfinite induction on the order type of the set of classes.

Surreal exponents. For $G=\mathbf{No}$, Conway's construction of a surreal number between two small sets supplies the required cofinalities and fills the cuts that make every quotient $\mathbf{No}/C$ Cauchy complete. Conway normal form carries the refinement property back to the omnific integers; moreover every irreducible omnific integer is prime.

phases.title: Two primality criteria
phases.description:
Two lemmas of commutative algebra carry primality from simpler rings to the rings of interest; both are used in the reduction along Archimedean classes. The first is a transfer lemma for a $D+M$ construction. Let $A$ be an integral domain and an $L$-algebra, $\pi:A\to L$ a homomorphism of $L$-algebras, and $S\subseteq L$ a subring. An element of $\pi^{-1}(S)$ is primal there as soon as it is primal in $A$ and either its residue is primal in $S$, or its residue is $0$ and $L$ is the fraction field of $S$. It is applied with $A=L((\Gamma^{\le0}))_\kappa$ and $\pi$ the constant coefficient.

The second lemma deduces primality in an integral domain $T$ from primality in a quotient $T/J$, using a family of idempotent ring endomorphisms that eventually kill each element of $J$ and after which divisibility can be tested. It is applied with $J$ the ideal of series whose support is bounded away from $0$, so that $T/J$ is a ring of germs, and with the restrictions of supports to Archimedean balls.

phases.title: Germs of translated truncations
phases.description:
Let $K$ be a field and $G$ a nontrivial ordered abelian group, and let $J$ be the ideal of series in $K((G^{\le0}))$ whose support is bounded away from $0$. For a series $b$ and an exponent $\gamma$, the germ of $b$ at $\gamma$ is the class modulo $J$ of the translated truncation $b^{|\gamma}=t^{-\gamma}b_{|\gamma}$ [Ber00, Def. 6.1]. This chapter proves the properties of germs on which the polynomial presentation rests. When $G$ is Cauchy complete for the group uniformity of its order topology, the germs of a product obey Berarducci's convolution formula, a finite sum over the decompositions $\gamma=\beta+(\gamma-\beta)$. The germs of $b^{|\gamma}$ at nonpositive exponents are the germs of $b$ translated by $\gamma$. The germ of $b$ at $\gamma$ is nonzero exactly when $\gamma$ lies in the closure of the support, and it is a constant exactly when the germs at all exponents in a left neighbourhood of $\gamma$ vanish.

The complexity that makes inductions possible is the Cantor--Bendixson rank of $0$ in the closure of the support, recorded as the ordinal $\omega^{\mathrm{rank}}$ and as $0$ when $0$ is not in the closed support. It vanishes exactly on $J$, it depends only on the germ, and when $0$ is in the closed support it strictly decreases when the series is replaced by its translated truncations at all exponents $\xi<0$ sufficiently close to $0$. The next chapter uses only these properties.

phases.title: Polynomial presentations
phases.description:
The properties of the preceding chapter are first isolated as axioms on a ring of series $A$ over a field $K$ of characteristic zero, with germ maps into a ring of germs $Q$. Fix a subalgebra $S\subseteq Q$ such that every element of $S$ is the germ of a series all of whose germs lie in $S$, and a series $X$ whose germs at negative exponents lie in $S$ while its germ $x$ does not. Applying the germ maps at negative exponents to a relation $ax+b=0$ and inducting on the rank of $a$ shows that no nonzero $a\in S$ has $ax\in S$. If $S$ is an integral domain, a polynomial relation for $x$ over $S$ of minimal degree is pushed through the germ maps; comparing the coefficients of the two highest powers of $x$, and using that $K$ has characteristic zero, reduces it to a relation of degree one between two series whose germs near $0$ are proportional, and an induction on rank excludes such proportionality. Hence $x$ is transcendental over $S$, and $S[x]$ again has the property assumed of $S$.

Transfinite adjunction of germs of minimal rank then presents the ring of germs $K((G^{\le0}))/J$ as a polynomial ring over $K$ for every Cauchy-complete ordered abelian group $G$; each intermediate stage is a polynomial ring and therefore an integral domain, so primality of $J$ is a consequence rather than an input. The same holds for series whose support has cardinality less than $\kappa$. For real exponents, the series all of whose germs are constants are exactly the series with finite support, and the same adjunction carried out with subalgebras of series closed under truncation presents $K((\mathbb R^{\le0}))$ as a polynomial ring over its finite-support subring $K(\mathbb R^{\le0})$. Since $K(\mathbb R^{\le0})$ is a GCD domain [LM24, Fact 2.5.2], Gauss's lemma makes $K((\mathbb R^{\le0}))$ a GCD domain. The reduction along Archimedean classes uses the GCD theorem at each class and the polynomial presentation of germs at limits of classes.

phases.title: Reduction along Archimedean classes
phases.description:
Let $G$ be an ordered vector space over an Archimedean ordered field, $R$ a field of characteristic zero, $Z\subseteq R$ a pre-Schreier subring and $\kappa$ an uncountable regular cardinal. For a convex subspace $C$ of $G$, regrouping exponents along a complement of $C$ writes $Z+R((G^{<0}))_\kappa$ as the $D+M$ construction $D+L((\Gamma^{<0}))_\kappa$ inside $T=L((\Gamma^{\le0}))_\kappa$, where $\Gamma=G/C$, $L=R((C))_\kappa$ and $D=Z+R((C^{<0}))_\kappa$; the constant coefficient of a regrouped series is its restriction to $C$. The transfer lemma therefore makes a series primal as soon as its regrouping is primal in $T$, its restriction to $C$ is primal in $D$, and $L$ is the fraction field of $D$ if that restriction vanishes. Restriction of supports to a convex subgroup is a ring endomorphism after which divisibility can be tested, and it splits off a factor with constant coefficient $1$.

The induction runs on the order type of the set of Archimedean classes met by the support. If this set is finite, take $C=G_{\prec\sigma}$ for the class $\sigma$ of the order of the series: the regrouped series has exponents in the image of $G_{\preceq\sigma}$, which is a copy of $\mathbb R$, and it is primal by the GCD theorem for real exponents, while the restriction to $C$ meets fewer classes. Otherwise the classes split into an initial segment $T_0$ without least element in magnitude and a finite final segment; take $C=\bigcap_{\sigma\in T_0}G_{\preceq\sigma}$. If $G/C$ is Cauchy complete, every germ in $T$ is primal, and restriction to the Archimedean balls of $G/C$ met by the support splits off factors of smaller order type, so the second primality criterion applies. The resulting theorem requires (A1)$_\sigma$ and (A2)$_\sigma$ of [LM24, Thm. 9.0.1] at every class, the analogous cofinality condition at the intersections $C$, and Cauchy completeness of the quotients $G/C$. The chapter ends with the observation that refinement forces $R$ to be the fraction field of $Z$.

phases.title: Surreal numbers and omnific integers
phases.description:
The last chapter checks the hypotheses of the general theorem for surreal exponents and returns to omnific integers. For every nonzero Archimedean class $\sigma$, each complement $H_\sigma$ of $\mathbf{No}_{\prec\sigma}$ in $\mathbf{No}_{\preceq\sigma}$ is isomorphic to $\mathbb R$. Conway's construction of a surreal number $\{L\mid R\}$ between two small sets gives the cofinality of the balls $\mathbf{No}_{\prec\sigma}$ and of the intersections $H_T$ of balls along small limit families, and it fills small cuts.

A cut criterion turns the filling of cuts into Cauchy completeness: given a Cauchy filter, choose points in sets of successively smaller diameter along a coinitial family of positive scales; the chosen points give the two sides of a cut, and a point filling the cut is a limit of the filter. Since cuts in $\mathbf{No}/H_T$ lift to cuts in $\mathbf{No}$, every such quotient is Cauchy complete. The general theorem then makes every element of $\mathbb Z+\mathbb R((\mathbf{No}^{<0}))_\kappa$ primal. Conway normal form with reversed exponents identifies this ring with the omnific integers, which therefore have the refinement property, and every irreducible omnific integer is prime.
